statement: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $S \subseteq R$ a multiplicative subset with $1 \in S$. If $M \xrightarrow{f} N \xrightarrow{g} P$ is [exact](c:exact-sequence) at $N$, then $S^{-1}M \to S^{-1}N \to S^{-1}P$ is exact at $S^{-1}N$. Localization also keeps injective and surjective maps, so it keeps every short exact sequence.

hypotheses.text: The sets $M$, $N$ and $P$ are [modules](c:module) over $R$, and $f$ and $g$ are $R$-[linear maps](c:linear-map).
The set $S$ contains $1$ and is closed under multiplication, so [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) at $S$ is defined. It may contain $0$.
The sequence is [exact](c:exact-sequence) at $N$: $\operatorname{im} f = \ker g$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{im}(S^{-1}f) = \ker(S^{-1}g)$. If $f$ is injective, then $S^{-1}f$ is injective. If $g$ is surjective, then $S^{-1}g$ is surjective.

formal.difference: The declaration states the exactness at $N$ for the localized maps. This record also states the injective and surjective cases and the short exact sequence.

proofs.name: Fractions and kernels
proofs.slogan: Compute with fractions: a kernel element has a multiple that lies in the image, and exactness lifts it.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any $S$ with $1 \in S$. If $0 \in S$, every localized module is $0$ and the claims hold at once.

roles.why: The maps are $R$-linear, so they commute with the action of $S$ on fractions.
Elements of $S$ are the denominators, and a fraction is zero when some element of $S$ kills its numerator.
Exactness at $N$ supplies the preimage that proves the reverse inclusion.

steps.slogan: Define the induced map on fractions and show that it is well defined.
steps.detail: Let $(S^{-1}f)(m/s) = f(m)/s$. If $m/s = n/t$, then $u(tm - sn) = 0$ for some $u \in S$. Linearity gives $u(tf(m) - sf(n)) = 0$, so the images are equal. Since $gf = 0$, the image of $S^{-1}f$ lies in the kernel of $S^{-1}g$.

steps.slogan: Lift a kernel element of $S^{-1}g$ to a fraction in the source.
steps.detail: Let $g(n)/s = 0$. Then $u\,g(n) = 0$ for some $u \in S$, so $g(un) = 0$. Exactness gives $m$ with $f(m) = un$. Hence $(S^{-1}f)(m/(us)) = un/(us) = n/s$, and the kernel lies in the image.

steps.slogan: Check that injective and surjective maps stay injective and surjective.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be injective and $f(m)/s = 0$. Then $f(um) = 0$ for some $u \in S$, so $um = 0$ and $m/s = 0$. Let $g$ be surjective and $p \in P$. Choose $n$ with $g(n) = p$. Then $n/s$ maps to $p/s$.

steps.slogan: Apply the three results to the maps of a short exact sequence.
steps.detail: The equality of image and kernel, the injective end and the surjective end all persist. Thus the localized sequence is short exact. If $0 \in S$, every fraction equals $0$ and the same conclusions hold.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Localization needs a commutative ring so that fractions can be added and compared.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness at $N$ is the hypothesis, and exactness after localization is the conclusion.
concepts.c:module: The fractions $m/s$ are elements of the localized modules.
concepts.c:linear-map: Linearity makes the induced map on fractions well defined.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: Equality of fractions uses an element of $S$ that kills the difference.

statement:
Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be open and $x_0 \in U$. Let $f = (f_1,\dots,f_m)\colon U 	o \mathbb{R}^m$ and $\varphi\colon U 	o \mathbb{R}$ be [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map). Put $S = \{x : f(x) = f(x_0)\}$. If $\varphi|_S$ has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $x_0$, then $\lambda_0
abla\varphi(x_0) + \sum_i \lambda_i 
abla f_i(x_0) = 0$ with real $\lambda_i$ not all $0$. If the [gradients](c:gradient) $
abla f_i(x_0)$ are [linearly independent](c:linear-independence), then $\lambda_0 = 1$ is possible.

hypotheses.text: The integers satisfy $n \ge 1$ and $0 \le m \le n$. For $m = 0$ the rule is $\nabla\varphi(x_0) = 0$.
The maps $f$ and $\varphi$ are [continuously differentiable](c:continuously-differentiable-map) on the open set $U$.
The restriction of $\varphi$ to $S$ has a [local extremum](c:local-extremum) at $x_0$.
For the normal form, the gradients $\nabla f_1(x_0),\dots,\nabla f_m(x_0)$ are [linearly independent](c:linear-independence).

conclusion:
There are real numbers $\lambda_0,\dots,\lambda_m$, not all $0$, with $\lambda_0
abla\varphi(x_0) + \sum \lambda_i
abla f_i(x_0) = 0$. Under independence of the $
abla f_i(x_0)$, one can take $\lambda_0 = 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the multiplier rule for strictly differentiable maps in normed spaces. This record states it for $C^1$ maps on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

proofs.name: Inverse function theorem
proofs.slogan: If the rows were independent, the inverse function theorem would give constrained points with larger and smaller values of the objective.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The case $m = 0$ is the rule $\nabla\varphi(x_0) = 0$ and needs no constraint.

roles.why: The dimension count $n - m - 1 \ge 0$ makes the extension of the matrix possible.
Continuous differentiability lets the inverse function theorem apply to the extended map.
A local extremum on $S$ is contradicted by points of $S$ on both sides of $\varphi(x_0)$.
Independence of the constraint gradients forces $\lambda_0 \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to linear dependence of the rows of one Jacobian matrix.
steps.detail:
Let $G = (f, \varphi)\colon U 	o \mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ and let $J$ be the matrix of $DG(x_0)$. Its rows are $
abla f_1(x_0),\dots,
abla f_m(x_0),
abla\varphi(x_0)$. A nontrivial vanishing combination of the rows is the claimed relation. So it is enough to show that the rows are dependent.

steps.slogan: Assume the rows are independent and extend $G$ to a map with invertible derivative.
steps.detail: Then $J$ has rank $m+1$, and its kernel $K$ has dimension $n - m - 1$. Choose a linear map $L$ that is an isomorphism on $K$. The map $x \mapsto (Jx, Lx)$ is injective, hence invertible. So $\hat G(x) = (G(x), Lx)$ is $C^1$ with invertible $D\hat G(x_0)$.

steps.slogan: Invert the extended map near $x_0$ and move only the value of $\varphi$.
steps.detail: The inverse function theorem gives a $C^1$ inverse near $y_0 = \hat G(x_0)$. For small real $t$, put $x_t = \hat G^{-1}(f(x_0), \varphi(x_0) + t, Lx_0)$. Then $f(x_t) = f(x_0)$, so $x_t \in S$, and $\varphi(x_t) = \varphi(x_0) + t$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the local extremum with points of $S$ on both sides.
steps.detail: The inverse is continuous, so $x_t \to x_0$ as $t \to 0$. Points of $S$ near $x_0$ have $\varphi > \varphi(x_0)$ for $t > 0$ and $\varphi < \varphi(x_0)$ for $t < 0$. This contradicts the extremum, so the rows of $J$ are dependent.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\lambda_0$ when the constraint gradients are independent.
steps.detail: In a nontrivial relation, $\lambda_0 = 0$ would give a nontrivial relation among the $\nabla f_i(x_0)$. This is impossible, so $\lambda_0 \ne 0$. Divide by $\lambda_0$ to get $\lambda_0 = 1$.

concepts.c:continuously-differentiable-map: The inverse function theorem needs a $C^1$ map.
concepts.c:local-extremum: The extremum on $S$ is the property that the constructed points contradict.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence of the constraint gradients rules out $\lambda_0 = 0$.
concepts.c:gradient: The gradients are the rows of the Jacobian matrix, and the relation is among them.

statement: Let $p$ be a prime and $G$ a group of order $p^2$. Then $G$ is abelian. Hence $G$ is isomorphic to the [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group) $\mathbb{Z}/p^2$ or to $\mathbb{Z}/p \times \mathbb{Z}/p$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite and $|G| = p^2$ for a prime $p$, so $G$ is a [p-group](c:p-group).

conclusion: The group $G$ is abelian, and $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/p^2$ or $G \cong \mathbb{Z}/p \times \mathbb{Z}/p$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only that a group of order $p^2$ is commutative. This record also lists the two isomorphism types.

proofs.name: Center and cyclic quotient
proofs.slogan: The center is not trivial; if it had order $p$, the quotient would be cyclic and the group abelian.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The order $p^3$ is excluded: the dihedral group of order $8$ is not abelian.

roles.why: The order $p^2$ makes $G$ a $p$-group and fixes the possible orders of the center and the quotient.

steps.slogan: Show that the [center](c:center) $Z$ of $G$ has order $p$ or $p^2$.
steps.detail: Because $G$ is a $p$-group, its center has order divisible by $p$. By Lagrange, $|Z| = p$ or $|Z| = p^2$. If $|Z| = p^2$, then $Z = G$ and $G$ is abelian.

steps.slogan: Suppose $|Z| = p$ and show that $G/Z$ is cyclic.
steps.detail: Then $|G/Z| = p$. A non-identity element of a group of prime order has order dividing $p$, so it has order $p$ and generates the group. Thus the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $G/Z$ is cyclic.

steps.slogan: Show that a cyclic quotient $G/Z$ makes $G$ abelian.
steps.detail: Let $gZ$ generate $G/Z$. Every $x$ has the form $g^i z$ with $z \in Z$. For $x = g^i z$ and $y = g^j z'$, we get $xy = g^{i+j} z z' = yx$, because central elements commute with all elements.

steps.slogan: Rule out $|Z| = p$ and conclude that $Z = G$.
steps.detail: By the lemma, $|Z| = p$ would make $G$ abelian. Then $Z = G$ and $|Z| = p^2$, which is a contradiction. So $|Z| = p^2$ and $G$ is abelian.

steps.slogan: Split by the largest element order to list the two isomorphism types.
steps.detail: If some $a$ has order $p^2$, then $G = \langle a \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/p^2$. Otherwise all non-identity elements have order $p$. Pick $a \ne e$ and $b \notin \langle a \rangle$. The map $(i,j) \mapsto a^i b^j$ is a homomorphism because $G$ is abelian. Its kernel is trivial, else $b \in \langle a \rangle$. Both groups have $p^2$ elements, so the map is an isomorphism.

concepts.c:cyclic-group: A cyclic quotient is the key to commutativity, and a cyclic $G$ is one outcome.
concepts.c:p-group: A $p$-group has a center of order divisible by $p$.
concepts.c:center: The center is the subgroup whose order the proof pins down.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The quotient $G/Z$ has prime order, so it is cyclic.

statement: Let $A$ be a subring of a commutative ring $B$. Let $N$ be a [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-module) $A$-submodule of $B$ that is faithful, for example one that contains $1$. If $b \in B$ satisfies $bN \subseteq N$, then $b$ is [integral](c:integral-extension) over $A$. Hence sums and products of integral elements are integral.

hypotheses.text: The ring $A$ is a subring of the commutative ring $B$.
The $A$-submodule $N \subseteq B$ is [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-module), and no nonzero element of $B$ kills $N$ (for example $1 \in N$).
The element $b \in B$ satisfies $bN \subseteq N$.

conclusion: The element $b$ is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$. Thus $b$ is integral over $A$, and the integral elements of $B$ form a subring.

formal.difference: The declaration proves that an element of a finitely generated subalgebra is integral. It does not state the module form with $bN \subseteq N$.

proofs.name: Determinant trick
proofs.slogan: Write the action of $b$ on the generators as a matrix; its characteristic polynomial kills $b$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Both cases of faithfulness are covered: $1 \in N$ and a general faithful $N$.

roles.why: The entries of the matrix lie in $A$, so the characteristic polynomial has coefficients in $A$.
A finite generating set gives a square matrix, and faithfulness turns $D N = 0$ into $D = 0$.
Stability under $b$ lets each product $b\,n_i$ be written with coefficients in $A$.

steps.slogan: Write the action of $b$ on generators as a matrix over $A$.
steps.detail: Let $n_1,\dots,n_k$ generate $N$. Since $bN \subseteq N$, write $b\,n_i = \sum_j m_{ij} n_j$ with $m_{ij} \in A$. Let $M = (m_{ij})$ and let $v$ be the column of the $n_j$. Then $(bI - M)v = 0$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by the [adjugate matrix](c:adjugate-matrix) to kill each generator.
steps.detail: Over a commutative ring, $\operatorname{adj}(X)X = \det(X) I$. With $X = bI - M$, this gives $D\,n_j = 0$ for $D = \det(bI - M)$ and every $j$.

steps.slogan: Show that $D$ kills all of $N$, hence $D = 0$.
steps.detail: $D$ kills every $A$-combination of the $n_j$, so $DN = 0$. If $1 \in N$, then $D = D \cdot 1 = 0$. If $N$ is faithful, then $D = 0$ by faithfulness.

steps.slogan: Expand the [determinant](c:determinant) as a monic polynomial in $b$.
steps.detail: Put $\chi(x) = \det(xI - M)$. This is a monic [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $k$ with coefficients in $A$, because the entries of $M$ are in $A$. Step 3 gives $\chi(b) = D = 0$, so $b$ is integral.

steps.slogan: Build a stable finitely generated module to show closure under sums and products.
steps.detail: Let $a$ and $b$ satisfy monic equations of degrees $r$ and $s$. Let $N$ be the $A$-span of $a^i b^j$ with $i < r$ and $j < s$. It contains $1$, and the monic equations show $aN \subseteq N$ and $bN \subseteq N$. So $(a+b)N \subseteq N$ and $(ab)N \subseteq N$, and the first part applies.

concepts.c:finitely-generated-module: A finite generating set gives a square matrix with a determinant.
concepts.c:integral-extension: Integrality is the conclusion: a monic equation over $A$.
concepts.c:adjugate-matrix: The adjugate turns a vanishing matrix-vector product into a vanishing determinant times each generator.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant of $bI - M$ gives the monic equation for $b$.
concepts.c:polynomial: The characteristic polynomial is monic with coefficients in $A$.

statement: Let $C$ be a [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real [vector space](c:vector-space) $E$ with $0 \in C$. Let $C$ be [absorbing](c:absorbing-subset): for each $x$ some $r > 0$ has $x \in rC$. Let $g(x) = \inf\{r > 0 : x \in rC\}$. Then $0 \le g < \infty$, $g(tx) = t\,g(x)$ for $t \ge 0$, $g(x+y) \le g(x)+g(y)$, and $\{g<1\} \subseteq C \subseteq \{g \le 1\}$. If $C$ is also balanced, $g$ is a [seminorm](c:seminorm).

hypotheses.text: The set $E$ is a real [vector space](c:vector-space) with no topology.
The set $C$ is [convex](c:convex-set), contains $0$ and is [absorbing](c:absorbing-subset).
For the seminorm claim, $C$ is also [balanced](c:balanced-set): $sC \subseteq C$ for $|s| \le 1$.

conclusion: The function $g$ is finite, positively homogeneous and subadditive, and $\{g<1\} \subseteq C \subseteq \{g \le 1\}$. If $C$ is balanced, $g$ is a seminorm.

formal.difference: The declaration states subadditivity of the gauge only. This record also states finiteness, homogeneity, the sandwich of $C$ and the seminorm case.

proofs.name: Convex combination with 0
proofs.slogan: Scaling up a convex set that contains 0 keeps the point inside; then convex combinations give subadditivity.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for the sandwich, homogeneity, subadditivity and the balanced case.

roles.why: Scalar multiples $rC$ and sums $x+y$ are formed in the vector space.
Convexity with $0 \in C$ gives monotone scaling, and absorbing makes $g$ finite.
Balancedness gives $sC = C$ for $|s| = 1$, so $g(sx) = g(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $x \in aC$ and $a < a'$ give $x \in a'C$.
steps.detail: We have $a^{-1}x \in C$. Then $a'^{-1}x = (a/a')(a^{-1}x) + (1 - a/a')\cdot 0$ is a convex combination of two points of $C$. So $a'^{-1}x \in C$.

steps.slogan: Show that $g$ is finite and nonnegative.
steps.detail: The set $\{r > 0 : x \in rC\}$ is nonempty because $C$ is absorbing, and it has only positive members. So $0 \le g(x) < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Scale the set of admissible radii to get positive homogeneity.
steps.detail: For $t > 0$, $tx \in rC$ if and only if $x \in (r/t)C$. So $g(tx) = t\,g(x)$. For $t = 0$, $0 \in rC$ for all $r > 0$, so $g(0) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Write $x+y$ as a convex combination to prove subadditivity.
steps.detail: Let $a > g(x)$ and $b > g(y)$. By step 1, $x \in aC$ and $y \in bC$. Then $x+y = (a+b)\big[\tfrac{a}{a+b}\tfrac{x}{a} + \tfrac{b}{a+b}\tfrac{y}{b}\big]$, and the bracket lies in $C$ by convexity. So $g(x+y) \le a+b$. Let $a \downarrow g(x)$ and $b \downarrow g(y)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the set $C$ with the sublevel sets of $g$.
steps.detail: If $g(x) < 1$, then $x \in rC$ for some $r < 1$, so $x \in C$ by step 1. If $x \in C$, then $1$ is an admissible radius, so $g(x) \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Collect the properties, and use balancedness to get $g(sx) = |s|g(x)$.
steps.detail: If $|s| = 1$, then $sC \subseteq C$ and $s^{-1}C \subseteq C$, so $sC = C$ and $g(sx) = g(x)$. With homogeneity, $g(sx) = |s|\,g(x)$. With subadditivity, $g$ is a [seminorm](c:seminorm).

concepts.c:vector-space: Sums, scalar multiples and the sets $rC$ live in the vector space.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity gives the monotone scaling and the convex combination for subadditivity.
concepts.c:absorbing-subset: Absorbing makes the set of admissible radii nonempty, so $g$ is finite.
concepts.c:balanced-set: Balancedness makes $g$ invariant under unit scalars.
concepts.c:seminorm: Homogeneity and subadditivity are exactly the seminorm axioms.

statement: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The series $e^{tA} = \sum_{k \ge 0} t^kA^k/k!$ converges for every real $t$. Its sum, the [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential), satisfies $\tfrac{d}{dt}e^{tA} = Ae^{tA} = e^{tA}A$ and $e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA}e^{tA}$. The function $x(t) = e^{tA}x_0$ is the only differentiable solution of the [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem) $x' = Ax$, $x(0) = x_0$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is constant. It does not depend on $t$.
The solution is required on an interval that contains $0$, for example on $\mathbb{R}$.
The matrix norm is an [operator norm](c:operator-norm), so $\|XY\| \le \|X\|\|Y\|$.

conclusion: The series converges, $e^{tA}$ is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA} = Ae^{tA}$, the group law holds, and $e^{tA}x_0$ is the unique solution with initial value $x_0$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the derivative of $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ in a normed algebra. This record also states uniqueness of the solution and the group law.

proofs.name: Termwise derivative and integrating factor
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the series term by term, then multiply a solution by $e^{-tA}$ to show that it is constant.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, on any interval that contains $0$. Uniqueness is proved for differentiable solutions without a size condition.

roles.why: A constant $A$ commutes with every power of itself, which gives $Ae^{tA} = e^{tA}A$.
The initial value at $t = 0$ and the zero derivative on an interval give uniqueness.
Submultiplicativity bounds the terms of the series by a scalar exponential series.

steps.slogan: Bound the series by a scalar exponential series and show uniform convergence.
steps.detail: By submultiplicativity, $\|t^kA^k/k!\| \le (|t|\|A\|)^k/k!$. The scalar series converges to $e^{|t|\|A\|}$. So the matrix series converges absolutely, and the partial sums converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on every $[-T, T]$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the series term by term to get $d/dt\, e^{tA} = Ae^{tA}$.
steps.detail: The $k$-th term has derivative $t^{k-1}A^k/(k-1)!$, and the derivative series is $A\sum_j t^jA^j/j!$. It converges uniformly on $[-T,T]$. So the termwise derivative is valid, and the factor $A$ can stand on either side. Then $x(t) = e^{tA}x_0$ solves $x' = Ax$ with $x(0) = x_0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $e^{-tA}$ is the inverse of $e^{tA}$.
steps.detail: Put $h(t) = e^{tA}e^{-tA}$. The product rule gives $h'(t) = Ae^{tA}e^{-tA} - e^{tA}Ae^{-tA} = 0$, because $A$ commutes with $e^{tA}$. So $h$ is constant, and $h(0) = I$.

steps.slogan: Multiply any solution by $e^{-tA}$ and show that the product is constant.
steps.detail: Let $y$ solve the problem and put $z(t) = e^{-tA}y(t)$. Then $z' = -Ae^{-tA}y + e^{-tA}Ay = 0$. A differentiable function with zero derivative on an interval is constant, so $z(t) = z(0) = x_0$. Hence $y(t) = e^{tA}x_0$ by step 3.

steps.slogan: Compare two solutions of the same problem to get the group law.
steps.detail: Fix $s$. The functions $Y_1(t) = e^{(t+s)A}$ and $Y_2(t) = e^{tA}e^{sA}$ both satisfy $Y' = AY$ and have value $e^{sA}$ at $t = 0$. Their columns solve the same initial value problems, so they agree by step 4. Hence $e^{(t+s)A} = e^{tA}e^{sA}$.

concepts.c:matrix-exponential: The proof studies the sum of this series and its derivative.
concepts.c:initial-value-problem: Existence and uniqueness of the solution of this problem is the main claim.
concepts.c:operator-norm: Submultiplicativity of the norm bounds the matrix powers.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence of the derivative series allows termwise differentiation.

statement: Let $H_n = 1 + 1/2 + \dots + 1/n$ be the [harmonic number](c:harmonic-number). Put $a_n = H_n - \ln(n+1)$ and $b_n = H_n - \ln n$. Then $a_n$ is strictly increasing, $b_n$ is strictly decreasing, and $b_n - a_n = \ln(1 + 1/n) \to 0$. Both [sequences](c:monotone-sequence) have the same [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $\gamma$, and $a_n < \gamma < b_m$ for all $n, m \ge 1$. Also $0 < b_n - \gamma < 1/n$.

hypotheses.text: The indices $n$ and $m$ are positive integers.
The symbol $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.

conclusion: The sequences $a_n$ and $b_n$ converge to the same limit $\gamma$, with $a_n < \gamma < b_m$ and $0 < b_n - \gamma < \ln(1 + 1/n) < 1/n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the sequence $H_n - \ln n$ is strictly decreasing. This record states both sequences and the error bound.

proofs.name: Monotone sandwich
proofs.slogan: Bound the logarithm by the mean value theorem, then trap the limit between an increasing and a decreasing sequence.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for all positive integers $n$ and $m$.

roles.why: Consecutive indices $n$ and $n+1$ give the differences of the sequences.
The logarithm is differentiable, so the mean value theorem applies to it.

steps.slogan: Bound $\ln(1+1/n)$ between $1/(n+1)$ and $1/n$.
steps.detail: By the mean value theorem, $\ln(n+1) - \ln n = 1/\xi$ for some $\xi \in (n, n+1)$. So $1/(n+1) < \ln(1 + 1/n) < 1/n$.

steps.slogan: Compare consecutive terms to show that $a_n$ increases and $b_n$ decreases.
steps.detail: We have $a_{n+1} - a_n = 1/(n+1) - \ln(1 + 1/(n+1))$, which is positive by the upper bound of step 1 at $n+1$. Also $b_{n+1} - b_n = 1/(n+1) - \ln(1 + 1/n)$, which is negative by the lower bound.

steps.slogan: Compute the gap $b_n - a_n$ and show that it tends to $0$.
steps.detail: The gap is $b_n - a_n = \ln(n+1) - \ln n = \ln(1 + 1/n)$. It is positive and tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Trap both sequences between $a_1$ and $b_1$ to get one common limit.
steps.detail: We have $a_1 \le a_n < b_n \le b_1$, so both sequences are bounded and monotone. They converge to $A$ and $B$. Since $b_n - a_n \to 0$, $A = B$. Call it $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Turn strict monotonicity into strict bounds and an error bound.
steps.detail: Since $a_n$ strictly increases to $\gamma$, $a_n < a_{n+1} \le \gamma$. Since $b_n$ strictly decreases to $\gamma$, $\gamma \le b_{n+1} < b_n$. So $a_n < \gamma < b_m$. Then $b_n - \gamma < b_n - a_n = \ln(1 + 1/n) < 1/n$ by step 1.

concepts.c:harmonic-number: The sequences are defined from the harmonic numbers.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The constant $\gamma$ is the common limit of both sequences.

statement: Let $s \notin \{0, -1, -2, \dots\}$. Then the [gamma function](c:gamma-function) satisfies $\Gamma(s) = \lim_{n \to \infty} n^s\, n!/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n))$. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, also $\Gamma(s) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^n (1 - t/n)^n t^{s-1}\,dt$, and the $n$-th integral equals $n^s B(s, n+1)$ for the [Beta function](c:euler-beta-function) $B$.

hypotheses.text: The function $\Gamma(s)$ is the [improper integral](c:improper-integral) $\int_0^\infty e^{-t}t^{s-1}dt$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. For other $s$, it is the [meromorphic](c:meromorphic-function) continuation, with $\Gamma(s+1) = s\Gamma(s)$.
The power $n^s$ means $\exp(s \ln n)$ for $n \ge 1$.
The limit runs over the integers $n$.

conclusion: For every $s$ that is not a pole, $\Gamma(s) = \lim n^s n!/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n))$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the Gauss limit formula for the sequence $\mathrm{GammaSeq}$ in the same range of $s$. This record also gives the integral form and the Beta integral.

proofs.name: Dominated convergence and Beta integral
proofs.slogan: Pass to the limit in the truncated integral, evaluate it as a Beta integral, then extend by the recursion.
proofs.scope: The case $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ by the integral, then all other non-pole $s$ by the recursion.

roles.why: The integral form gives $\Gamma$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, and the recursion gives it elsewhere.
The factor $n^s$ appears when the integral is rescaled by $t = nu$.
The limit in $n$ is the limit in the dominated convergence step and in the recursion.

steps.slogan: Truncate the integrand at $n$ and bound it by $e^{-t}t^{\operatorname{Re}s-1}$.
steps.detail: For $\operatorname{Re}s > 0$, put $f_n(t) = (1 - t/n)^n t^{s-1}$ for $0 < t < n$ and $f_n(t) = 0$ for $t \ge n$. For $0 \le t < n$, $0 \le 1 - t/n \le e^{-t/n}$, so $(1-t/n)^n \le e^{-t}$. Thus $|f_n(t)| \le e^{-t}t^{\operatorname{Re}s-1}$, which is integrable.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit under the integral by dominated convergence.
steps.detail: For fixed $t$, $(1 - t/n)^n \to e^{-t}$, so $f_n(t) \to e^{-t}t^{s-1}$. The bound of step 1 and dominated convergence give $\int_0^n(1-t/n)^n t^{s-1}dt = \int_0^\infty f_n \to \Gamma(s)$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $t = nu$ to turn the integral into $n^s B(s, n+1)$.
steps.detail: The factor $n^s$ comes out of the integral, and the limits become $0$ and $1$. We get $\int_0^n(1-t/n)^n t^{s-1}dt = n^s\int_0^1(1-u)^n u^{s-1}du = n^s B(s, n+1)$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the Beta integral by parts $n$ times.
steps.detail: The boundary terms $[u^s(1-u)^n/s]_0^1$ vanish, so $B(s, n+1) = (n/s)B(s+1, n)$. Repeat $n$ times and use $B(s+n, 1) = 1/(s+n)$. Then $B(s, n+1) = n!/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n))$. So $G_n(s) := n^s n!/(s\cdots(s+n)) \to \Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re}s > 0$.

steps.slogan: Relate $G_n(s)$ to $G_n(s+1)$ by a direct computation.
steps.detail: From the definition, $G_n(s) = G_n(s+1)\,(s+n+1)/(sn)$, valid when $s, s+1, \dots, s+n+1$ are nonzero.

steps.slogan: Extend the limit to all non-pole $s$ by the recursion of $\Gamma$.
steps.detail: Choose $m \ge 0$ with $\operatorname{Re}(s+m) > 0$. Then $G_n(s+m) \to \Gamma(s+m)$ by step 4. Use step 5 repeatedly. Each factor $(s+j+n+1)/n$ tends to $1$, so $G_n(s+j) \to \Gamma(s+j+1)/(s+j) = \Gamma(s+j)$. Go from $j = m-1$ down to $j = 0$.

concepts.c:gamma-function: The theorem expresses $\Gamma$ as a limit of explicit products.
concepts.c:euler-beta-function: The rescaled truncated integral is a Beta integral with a closed form.
concepts.c:improper-integral: The definition of $\Gamma$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ is an improper integral.
concepts.c:meromorphic-function: Outside $\operatorname{Re}s > 0$, $\Gamma$ is defined by meromorphic continuation.

statement: Let $P$ and $Q$ be posets and $l\colon P \to Q$, $u\colon Q \to P$ maps with $l(a) \le b \iff a \le u(b)$. This pair is a [Galois connection](c:galois-connection). Then $a \le ul(a)$ and $lu(b) \le b$; $l$ and $u$ are monotone; $lul = l$ and $ulu = u$; $ul$ is a [closure operator](c:closure-operator); $l$ and $u$ give inverse order isomorphisms between the closed elements; and $l$ sends every existing [join](c:least-upper-bound) to a join.

hypotheses.text: The sets $P$ and $Q$ are partially ordered. Preorders suffice for parts 1 and 2.
The pair $(l, u)$ is a [Galois connection](c:galois-connection): $l(a) \le b \iff a \le u(b)$ for all $a \in P$ and $b \in Q$.
In part 6, the join exists in $P$ for the chosen subset. No completeness of $P$ or $Q$ is needed.

conclusion: Parts 1 to 6 hold: unit and counit inequalities, monotonicity, $lul = l$ and $ulu = u$, $ul$ is a closure operator, the isomorphism of closed elements, and preservation of joins by $l$ and meets by $u$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the unit inequality $a \le u(l(a))$. This record states all six parts.

proofs.name: Unit, counit and adjunction
proofs.slogan: Insert the trivial inequalities into the equivalence to get unit and counit, then derive every other part from them.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The same proof gives the polarity form with an antitone pair, after the order on $Q$ is reversed.

roles.why: Antisymmetry of the order gives equalities from two inequalities in parts 3 and 5.
The equivalence is the only tool: every part is derived from it.
A join of a subset is a least upper bound, which is what part 6 compares.

steps.slogan: Insert $b = l(a)$ and $a = u(b)$ into the equivalence to get unit and counit.
steps.detail: Put $b = l(a)$. Since $l(a) \le l(a)$, we get $a \le u(l(a))$. Put $a = u(b)$. Since $u(b) \le u(b)$, we get $l(u(b)) \le b$.

steps.slogan: Combine unit and counit with the equivalence to show that $l$ and $u$ are monotone.
steps.detail: Let $a \le a'$. Then $a \le a' \le ul(a')$, and the equivalence gives $l(a) \le l(a')$. Let $b \le b'$. Then $lu(b) \le b \le b'$, and the equivalence gives $u(b) \le u(b')$.

steps.slogan: Show that $lul = l$ and $ulu = u$ by two opposite inequalities.
steps.detail: Monotonicity of $l$ applied to $a \le ul(a)$ gives $l(a) \le lul(a)$. The counit at $b = l(a)$ gives $lul(a) \le l(a)$. So $lul = l$. The identity $ulu = u$ follows in the same way.

steps.slogan: Verify that $ul$ is extensive, monotone and idempotent, and least above $a$.
steps.detail: Extensive is part 1, and monotone holds for a composite of monotone maps. Idempotent: $ulul(a) = u(lul(a)) = ul(a)$ by step 3. If $a \le u(q)$, the equivalence gives $l(a) \le q$, and $u$ gives $ul(a) \le u(q)$. So $ul(a)$ is the least element of the form $u(q)$ above $a$.

steps.slogan: Restrict $l$ and $u$ to the closed elements and show that they invert each other.
steps.detail: If $a = ul(a)$, then $lul(a) = l(a)$ by step 3, so $l(a)$ is closed in $Q$. If $b = lu(b)$, then $u(b)$ is closed in $P$. On closed elements, $ul(a) = a$ and $lu(b) = b$. Both maps are monotone, so they are inverse order isomorphisms.

steps.slogan: Show that $l(j)$ is the least upper bound of $l(S)$ when $j$ is the join of $S$.
steps.detail: Since $l$ is monotone, $l(j)$ is an upper bound of $l(S)$. Let $b$ be any upper bound of $l(S)$. For each $x \in S$, $l(x) \le b$, so $x \le u(b)$. Then $j \le u(b)$ and $l(j) \le b$. The case of meets and $u$ is the dual.

steps.slogan: Collect the six parts as the statement of the theorem.
steps.detail: Step 1 is part 1, step 2 is part 2, step 3 is part 3, step 4 is part 4, step 5 is part 5, and step 6 is part 6. All parts follow from the equivalence alone.

concepts.c:galois-connection: The equivalence defining the connection is the only hypothesis used.
concepts.c:closure-operator: The composite $ul$ has the three closure properties.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: Part 6 shows that $l$ maps a join to a join.

statement: Let $(X, Y)$ be a [jointly Gaussian](c:gaussian-measure) pair of real random variables: every combination $aX + bY$ has a [normal law](c:normal-distribution), possibly of variance $0$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) = 0$, then $X$ and $Y$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables). Hence, for i.i.d. normal $X_1,\dots,X_n$, the sample mean is independent of every residual $X_i - \bar X$ and of the sample variance.

hypotheses.text: The pair $(X, Y)$ is [jointly Gaussian](c:gaussian-measure). Two normal marginals are not enough.
The covariance is zero: $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$.
For the sample statement, $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d. with law $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

conclusion: The variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The sample mean $\bar X$ is independent of the residual vector and of the sample variance.

formal.difference: The declaration states the independence of two variables with a joint Gaussian law and zero covariance. This record also treats the sample mean and the sample variance.

proofs.name: Characteristic function factors
proofs.slogan: Compute the joint characteristic function from the normal law of each combination; zero covariance makes it a product.
proofs.scope: The pair statement, including degenerate normal laws, then the sample mean for i.i.d. normal variables.

roles.why: Every combination $sX + tY$ is normal, so its characteristic function is known.
Zero covariance removes the cross term from the variance of $sX + tY$.
The mean and the residuals are linear images of a Gaussian vector, so they are jointly Gaussian.

steps.slogan: Write the joint characteristic function from the normal law of $sX + tY$.
steps.detail: For real $s, t$, the variable $W = sX + tY$ is normal with mean $m_W = s\,EX + t\,EY$ and variance $v_W$. So the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) at 1 is $E e^{iW} = \exp(i m_W - v_W/2)$.

steps.slogan: Insert zero covariance into the variance and factor the exponential.
steps.detail: We have $v_W = s^2 \operatorname{Var}X + 2st\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y) + t^2\operatorname{Var}Y$. With zero covariance, $E e^{i(sX+tY)} = \exp(is\,EX - s^2\operatorname{Var}X/2)\exp(it\,EY - t^2\operatorname{Var}Y/2)$.

steps.slogan: Set $t = 0$ and $s = 0$ to identify the two factors as the marginal functions.
steps.detail: With $(s, 0)$, $X$ is normal with mean $EX$ and variance $\operatorname{Var}X$. With $(0, t)$, the same holds for $Y$. So the two factors are $\varphi_X(s)$ and $\varphi_Y(t)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude independence from the factorization of the characteristic function.
steps.detail: The joint characteristic function equals $\varphi_X(s)\varphi_Y(t)$ for all $(s, t)$. By the criterion for independence, $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

steps.slogan: Apply the pair result to the sample mean and the residual vector.
steps.detail: The vector $(\bar X, X_1 - \bar X, \dots, X_n - \bar X)$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, so it is jointly Gaussian. Since $\operatorname{Cov}(\bar X, X_i) = \sigma^2/n = \operatorname{Var}\bar X$, we get $\operatorname{Cov}(\bar X, X_i - \bar X) = 0$. Steps 1 to 4 with vector coefficients give that $\bar X$ is independent of the residuals, hence of their function $S^2$.

concepts.c:gaussian-measure: Joint Gaussianity gives a normal law for every linear combination.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: The characteristic function of a normal law is explicit.
concepts.c:characteristic-function: The factorization of this function is the route to independence.

statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be [i.i.d.](c:iid-random-variables) with $P(X_1 > x) = e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 0$. Let $M_n = \max_{k \le n} X_k$. Then almost surely the [limit superior](c:limit-superior) of $X_n/\ln n$ is $1$ and $\lim M_n/\ln n = 1$. For $c > 1$, almost surely $X_n \le c\ln n$ for all large $n$. For $c \le 1$, almost surely $X_n > c\ln n$ for infinitely many $n$.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_n$ are independent and identically distributed.
The tail is exactly exponential: $P(X_1 > x) = e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 0$.

conclusion: Almost surely $\limsup X_n/\ln n = 1$ and $M_n/\ln n \to 1$. The terms $X_n/\ln n$ do not converge to $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the almost sure value $\limsup X_n/\ln n = 1$ for a sequence with exponential tails. This record also states the limit of the maxima.

proofs.name: Borel-Cantelli dichotomy
proofs.slogan: The tail probabilities $n^{-c}$ have a convergent sum for $c > 1$ and a divergent sum for $c \le 1$, so the two Borel-Cantelli lemmas give the limsup.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Almost sure statements hold outside a null set; countably many such events are intersected.

roles.why: Independence is used in the second lemma and in $P(M_n \le x) = P(X_1 \le x)^n$.
The exact tail gives $P(X_n > c\ln n) = n^{-c}$.

steps.slogan: Compute the tail probabilities $P(X_n > c\ln n) = n^{-c}$.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 2$ and $c > 0$, $P(X_n > c\ln n) = e^{-c\ln n} = n^{-c}$. The sum $\sum n^{-c}$ converges for $c > 1$ and diverges for $c \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Use the first lemma to bound the limsup by $1$.
steps.detail: For $c > 1$, $\sum n^{-c} < \infty$. The first Borel-Cantelli lemma shows that $X_n > c\ln n$ happens only finitely often almost surely. Intersect these events for $c = 1 + 1/j$, $j = 1, 2, \dots$ Then $\limsup X_n/\ln n \le 1$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Use the second lemma to show that $X_n > c\ln n$ occurs infinitely often for $c \le 1$.
steps.detail: The events $\{X_n > \ln n\}$ are independent, and $\sum 1/n = \infty$. The second lemma shows that they occur infinitely often almost surely. For $0 < c \le 1$, $X_n > \ln n$ implies $X_n > c\ln n$. For $c \le 0$, $P(X_n > 0) = 1$. With step 2, $\limsup X_n/\ln n = 1$.

steps.slogan: Bound $M_n/\ln n$ from above for large $n$.
steps.detail: Take $c > 1$ and an outcome outside the null set of step 2. There is $K$ with $X_k \le c\ln k$ for $k \ge K$. Then $M_n \le \max(M_K, c\ln n)$ for $n \ge K$. So $\limsup M_n/\ln n \le c$. Let $c \downarrow 1$ along $1 + 1/j$.

steps.slogan: Bound $M_n/\ln n$ from below by the first lemma.
steps.detail: Let $0 < c < 1$. By independence, $P(M_n \le c\ln n) = (1 - n^{-c})^n \le \exp(-n^{1-c})$. For large $n$, this is at most $n^{-2}$, which is summable. The first lemma gives $M_n > c\ln n$ for large $n$ almost surely. Let $c \uparrow 1$. Steps 4 and 5 give $M_n/\ln n \to 1$. The single terms do not converge, since $\{X_n < 1\}$ are independent events of probability $1 - e^{-1}$ that occur infinitely often.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independence and equal law give the product formula for $P(M_n \le x)$ and the second lemma.
concepts.c:limit-superior: The theorem identifies the limit superior of $X_n/\ln n$.

statement: Let $R$ be a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain) and $A$ an $m \times n$ matrix of rank $r$ over $R$. There are invertible $U$, $V$ with $UAV = D$, where $D$ has diagonal entries $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \dots \mid d_r$, all nonzero, and zeros elsewhere. This is the [Smith normal form](c:smith-normal-form). The $d_i$ are unique up to units, and $d_1\cdots d_k$ is the [gcd](c:greatest-common-divisor) of the $k \times k$ minors. The [cokernel](c:cokernel) of $A$ is $\bigoplus R/(d_i) \oplus R^{m-r}$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain) with Euclidean function $\delta$, so division with remainder works.
A matrix is invertible when it has an inverse over $R$. Equivalently, its [determinant](c:determinant) is a unit of $R$.
The uniqueness claim holds up to multiplication of each $d_i$ by a unit.

conclusion: There are invertible $U$, $V$ with $UAV$ in Smith normal form. The $d_i$ are unique up to units, $d_1\cdots d_k \sim \Delta_k(A)$, and $R^m/AR^n \cong \bigoplus R/(d_i) \oplus R^{m-r}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the existence of a Smith normal form for a submodule of a free module over a principal ideal domain. This record also states the determinantal divisors and the quotient.

proofs.name: Minimal pivot and minors
proofs.slogan: Choose a pivot of smallest size, clear its row and column by division, and read the invariants from the gcds of minors.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The zero matrix has rank $0$ and is already in normal form.

roles.why: Division with remainder and a size function drive the choice of the minimal pivot and the clearing steps.
Row and column operations are invertible matrices, and the minors transform by Cauchy-Binet.
The gcd of the minors is defined only up to a unit.

steps.slogan: Choose a nonzero entry of smallest size $\delta$ among all equivalent matrices.
steps.detail: Assume $A \ne 0$. Among all matrices equivalent to $A$, choose $B$ with a nonzero entry $b$ whose $\delta(b)$ is least, by well ordering. Swap rows and columns so that $b$ sits at position $(1,1)$.

steps.slogan: Divide each entry of the first row and column by $b$ and clear them.
steps.detail: Write $B_{1j} = qb + \rho$ with $\rho = 0$ or $\delta(\rho) < \delta(b)$. Subtract $q$ times column 1 from column $j$. A nonzero $\rho$ would contradict minimality, so $\rho = 0$. The column case is the same. Then $B = \operatorname{diag}(b, A')$.

steps.slogan: Show that the pivot $b$ divides every entry of $A'$.
steps.detail: Suppose $b \nmid a$ for an entry $a$ of $A'$ at $(i,j)$. Add row $i$ to row 1, so that row 1 holds $b$ and $a$. Write $a = qb + \rho$ with $\rho \ne 0$ and $\delta(\rho) < \delta(b)$. Subtract $q$ times column 1 from column $j$. This gives a smaller nonzero entry, which contradicts minimality.

steps.slogan: Repeat on the block $A'$ to build the divisibility chain.
steps.detail: Operations on $A'$ replace its entries by $R$-linear combinations of old entries, which stay multiples of $b$. Induction on the size gives $\operatorname{diag}(b, d_2, \dots, d_r, 0, \dots, 0)$ with $b \mid d_2$ and $d_i \mid d_{i+1}$. This proves existence.

steps.slogan: Show that the gcd $\Delta_k$ of the $k \times k$ minors does not change under $A \mapsto UAV$.
steps.detail: By Cauchy-Binet, each $k \times k$ minor of $UAV$ is an $R$-linear combination of $k \times k$ minors of $A$. So $\Delta_k(A) \mid \Delta_k(UAV)$. Apply this to $A = U^{-1}(UAV)V^{-1}$ to get the opposite divisibility. Thus the two agree up to a unit.

steps.slogan: Compute $\Delta_k(D)$ from the chain and read off the uniqueness of the $d_i$.
steps.detail: A $k \times k$ minor of $D$ is zero unless its row and column sets agree. Then it is $d_{i_1}\cdots d_{i_k}$ with $i_t \ge t$, and $d_t \mid d_{i_t}$ by the chain. So $\Delta_k(D) = d_1 \cdots d_k$ up to a unit. By step 5, $d_k \sim \Delta_k(A)/\Delta_{k-1}(A)$.

steps.slogan: Transport the column space by $U$ and read off the quotient and its size.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto Ux$ sends $AR^n$ onto $UAVR^n = DR^n$. So $R^m/AR^n \cong R^m/DR^n \cong \bigoplus R/(d_i) \oplus R^{m-r}$. For $R = \mathbb{Z}$ and $m = n = r$, the order is $\prod |d_i|$. Since $\det U, \det V = \pm 1$, this equals $|\det A|$.

concepts.c:euclidean-domain: Division with remainder is the only property of the ring that the proof uses.
concepts.c:determinant: Invertible matrices over $R$ are those with unit determinant, and minors are determinants.
concepts.c:smith-normal-form: This diagonal form is what the first part constructs.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: The gcd of the minors is the invariant that fixes the $d_i$.
concepts.c:cokernel: The quotient $R^m/AR^n$ is the cokernel of $A$.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) of degree $n$ with $r_2$ pairs of complex embeddings and [discriminant](c:discriminant) $d_K$. Put $M_K = \frac{n!}{n^n}(4/\pi)^{r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}$. Every class of the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) contains an integral ideal $I$ with $N(I) \le M_K$. So the class group is finite, and it is generated by the classes of prime ideals of norm at most $M_K$. If $M_K < 2$, the class number is $1$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field) with $n = r_1 + 2r_2$.
The ring of integers $O_K$ is a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain): an ideal contains $(\alpha)$ if and only if it divides $(\alpha)$.
The absolute norm $N(I) = |O_K/I|$ is multiplicative on ideals, and $N((\alpha)) = |N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)|$.

conclusion: Every ideal class has an integral ideal of norm at most $M_K$. Hence the class group is finite, it is generated by primes $P$ with $N(P) \le M_K$, and $M_K < 2$ gives class number $1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the existence of an integral ideal of norm at most the Minkowski bound in each class. This record also states finiteness, generation by small primes and the case $M_K < 2$.

proofs.name: Convex body in the ideal lattice
proofs.slogan: Put the ideal in the Minkowski space as a lattice, find a short nonzero element in a convex body, and bound the norm by the arithmetic-geometric mean.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for any number field. The volume formula is proved by induction on the number of real and complex places.

roles.why: The embeddings place $O_K$ and its ideals as lattices in $\mathbb{R}^{r_1} \times \mathbb{C}^{r_2}$.
In a Dedekind domain, containing $(\alpha)$ means dividing it, so $(\alpha) = JI'$ for an integral $I'$.
Multiplicativity of the norm gives $N(J)N(I') = |N(\alpha)|$ and finiteness of ideals of bounded norm.

steps.slogan: Compute the covolume of the ideal lattice $\sigma(I)$ in Minkowski space.
steps.detail: Let $M = (\sigma_i(\omega_j))$ for a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis $\omega_j$ of $O_K$, so $d_K = \det(M)^2$. Replace each complex pair $z, \bar z$ by $\operatorname{Re} z, \operatorname{Im} z$. Each pair changes the determinant by a factor of modulus $1/2$. So $\sigma(O_K)$ has covolume $2^{-r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}$, and $\sigma(I)$ has covolume $2^{-r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}\,N(I)$, because its index is $N(I)$.

steps.slogan: Define the convex body $B_t$ and compute its volume by induction.
steps.detail: Let $B_t = \{(x,z) : \sum|x_i| + 2\sum|z_j| \le t\}$. It is compact, convex and symmetric, with volume $t^n V(1)$. Slicing off one real coordinate gives a factor $2/(m+1)$, and one complex coordinate gives a factor $(\pi/2)/((m+1)(m+2))$. Induction gives $V(1) = 2^{r_1}(\pi/2)^{r_2}/n!$.

steps.slogan: Choose $t$ so that the volume is $2^n$ times the covolume and find a lattice point.
steps.detail: Choose $t$ with $V(t) = 2^n \cdot 2^{-r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}\,N(I)$. Since $n - r_1 = 2r_2$, this gives $t^n = n!\,(4/\pi)^{r_2}\sqrt{|d_K|}\,N(I)$. The convex body theorem gives a nonzero $\alpha \in I$ with $\sigma(\alpha) \in B_t$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|N(\alpha)|$ by the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality.
steps.detail: The norm $|N(\alpha)|$ is the product of $n$ numbers, namely $|x_i|$ and twice $|z_j|$, whose sum is at most $t$. So $|N(\alpha)| \le (t/n)^n = M_K\,N(I)$.

steps.slogan: Find an integral ideal of norm at most $M_K$ in a given class.
steps.detail: Let $C$ be a class and $J$ an integral ideal in $C^{-1}$. Steps 3 and 4 give a nonzero $\alpha \in J$ with $|N(\alpha)| \le M_K N(J)$. Then $(\alpha) = JI'$ for an integral $I'$, and $N(J)N(I') = |N(\alpha)|$, so $N(I') \le M_K$. In the class group, $[I'] = [J]^{-1} = C$.

steps.slogan: Factor $I'$ into primes to get generation, finiteness and the case $M_K < 2$.
steps.detail: Each prime factor $P$ of $I'$ has $N(P) \le M_K$, and $N(P) = p^f \ge p$ for the prime $p$ below it. So the small primes generate the class group. An ideal of norm $N$ divides $(N)$, which has finitely many divisors, so the class group is finite. If $M_K < 2$, then $N(I) = 1$, so $I = O_K$.

concepts.c:number-field: The embeddings of $K$ define Minkowski space and the lattice.
concepts.c:discriminant: The discriminant fixes the covolume of the lattice $\sigma(O_K)$.
concepts.c:ideal-class-group: The theorem bounds the norm of a representative in each class.
concepts.c:dedekind-domain: Dedekind arithmetic turns containment into divisibility of ideals.

statement: Let $J$ be an interval, $A\colon J \to \mathbb{K}^{n\times n}$ continuous and $X\colon J \to \mathbb{K}^{n \times n}$ a $C^1$ matrix function with $X' = AX$. Then $\det X(t) = \det X(t_0)\exp\big(\int_{t_0}^t \operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds\big)$ for all $t, t_0 \in J$. So $\det X$ vanishes at one point of $J$ or at none. For $n$ solutions of $x' = A(t)x$, the [Wronskian](c:wronskian) is identically $0$ or never $0$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix function $A$ is continuous on the interval $J$. No commutation property is needed.
The matrix $X$ is $C^1$ and satisfies $X'(t) = A(t)X(t)$ for all $t \in J$, so it is a [fundamental matrix](c:fundamental-matrix) when its determinant is nonzero.

conclusion: The determinant satisfies Liouville's formula, so it is either identically zero on $J$ or nonzero at every point of $J$.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the first-order expansion of $\det(1 + tA)$. This record states the full formula for a matrix solution and its consequences.

proofs.name: Derivative of a determinant
proofs.slogan: Show that the determinant solves the scalar equation $w' = (\operatorname{tr}A)\,w$ and integrate it.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The singular case, where $X$ is not invertible at some point, is handled by a separate uniqueness argument.

roles.why: Continuity of $A$ makes $\operatorname{tr}A$ continuous, so its integral is a $C^1$ function and Gronwall applies.
The equation $X' = AX$ gives the first-order expansion of $X(t+h)$ and the vector solution $y = Xv$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\det(I + E)$ to first order in a small matrix $E$.
steps.detail: The identity permutation gives $\prod(1 + E_{ii}) = 1 + \operatorname{tr}E + \dots$ with terms of degree at least 2. Every other permutation moves two indices, so it has two off-diagonal factors. Hence $\det(I + E) = 1 + \operatorname{tr}E + R(E)$ with $|R(E)| \le C\|E\|^2$ for $\|E\| \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Compute $w'(t) = \operatorname{tr}A(t)\,w(t)$ at points where $X(t)$ is invertible.
steps.detail: Write $X(t+h) = (I + hA(t) + E(h))X(t)$ with $E(h) = o(h)$, because $X' = AX$. By multiplicativity, $w(t+h) = w(t)\det(I + hA(t) + E(h)) = w(t)(1 + h\operatorname{tr}A(t) + o(h))$ by step 1. So $w' = \operatorname{tr}A\cdot w$.

steps.slogan: Treat the singular case by uniqueness of the solution through zero.
steps.detail: Suppose $\det X(t_1) = 0$. Pick $v \ne 0$ with $X(t_1)v = 0$ and put $y = Xv$. Then $y' = Ay$ and $y(t_1) = 0$. The Gronwall bound with zero initial value gives $y \equiv 0$. So $X(t)v = 0$, $\det X \equiv 0$, and the formula holds with both sides $0$.

steps.slogan: Multiply $w$ by $e^{-a(t)}$ with $a(t) = \int_{t_0}^t \operatorname{tr}A$ to get a constant.
steps.detail: If $\det X(t) \ne 0$ on $J$, step 2 holds at every $t$. The function $a$ is $C^1$ with $a' = \operatorname{tr}A$. Then $(we^{-a})' = (w' - a'w)e^{-a} = 0$, so $w(t)e^{-a(t)} = w(t_0)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases and read off the dichotomy for the Wronskian.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 prove the formula for all $t, t_0 \in J$. The exponential never vanishes, so $\det X(t) = 0$ for one $t$ if and only if for all $t$. For $n$ solutions of $x' = A(t)x$ as columns, $\det X$ is the [Wronskian](c:wronskian).

concepts.c:wronskian: The determinant of a matrix of solutions is the Wronskian.
concepts.c:fundamental-matrix: An invertible matrix solution is a fundamental matrix.

statement: Let $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be continuous, $2\pi$-periodic and piecewise $C^1$. Put $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f'|^2$, and let $c_n$ be the Fourier coefficients of $f$. Then $\sum_{n \ne 0}|c_n| \le (\pi/\sqrt3)\,\sigma$. The [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) converges [absolutely](c:absolute-convergence) and [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) to $f$, and the partial sum of order $N$ has error at most $\sigma\sqrt{2/N}$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous and $2\pi$-periodic. A jump would give $c_n$ of size $1/n$.
There are $0 = x_0 < \dots < x_m = 2\pi$ such that $f$ is $C^1$ on each $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$. The values of $f'$ at the break points do not matter.

conclusion: The coefficients satisfy $\sum_{n \ne 0}|c_n| \le (\pi/\sqrt3)\sigma$, the series converges uniformly to $f$, and $\sup_x|f(x) - S_Nf(x)| \le \sigma\sqrt{2/N}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums. This record uses it to bound the Fourier series.

proofs.name: Parseval and Cauchy-Schwarz
proofs.slogan: Integrate by parts to relate the coefficients of $f'$ to those of $f$, then use Parseval for $f'$ and Cauchy-Schwarz.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, with bounds that hold for every $x$ and every $N \ge 1$.

roles.why: Continuity and periodicity cancel the boundary terms in the integration by parts and make $f - g$ continuous.
On each piece, integration by parts applies, and $f'$ is bounded and square integrable.

steps.slogan: Integrate by parts on each piece to get $c_n(f') = in\,c_n$.
steps.detail: On each piece, $\int f'e^{-inx}dx = [fe^{-inx}] + in\int fe^{-inx}dx$. Sum over the pieces. The boundary terms telescope because $f$ is continuous, and the end terms cancel because $f$ is periodic. So $c_n(f') = in\,c_n$.

steps.slogan: Apply Parseval to $f'$ to get $\sum n^2|c_n|^2 = \sigma^2$.
steps.detail: The function $f'$ is piecewise continuous and bounded, hence square integrable. Parseval gives $\sum_n |c_n(f')|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int|f'|^2 = \sigma^2$. By step 1, this is $\sum n^2|c_n|^2$.

steps.slogan: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to $\sum|c_n| = \sum (1/|n|)(|n||c_n|)$.
steps.detail: For $M \ge 1$, $\sum_{0<|n|\le M}|c_n| \le (\sum n^{-2})^{1/2}(\sum n^2|c_n|^2)^{1/2}$. The first factor is at most $(2\zeta(2))^{1/2} = \pi/\sqrt3$, and the second is at most $\sigma$ by step 2. Let $M \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that the series converges uniformly and that its sum is $f$.
steps.detail: The terms have modulus $|c_n|$, and $\sum|c_n| < \infty$ by step 3. The Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence to a continuous $g$. Termwise integration gives $c_n(g) = c_n(f)$. So $f - g$ is continuous with all coefficients $0$, and Parseval gives $\int|f-g|^2 = 0$. Hence $f = g$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tail $\sum_{|n|>N}|c_n|$ in the same way.
steps.detail: For every $x$, $|f(x) - S_Nf(x)| \le \sum_{|n|>N}|c_n|$. As in step 3, this is at most $(2\sum_{n>N}n^{-2})^{1/2}\sigma$. Since $\sum_{n>N}n^{-2} < \sum_{n>N}1/(n(n-1)) = 1/N$, the bound is $\sigma\sqrt{2/N}$.

concepts.c:fourier-series: The series of $f$ is the object whose convergence is proved.
concepts.c:absolute-convergence: The bound on $\sum|c_n|$ is absolute convergence.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: The M-test turns the summable bound into uniform convergence.

statement: Let $C \subseteq A^n$ be a [code](c:error-correcting-code) over an alphabet of $q \ge 2$ symbols, with $M \ge 2$ words and minimum Hamming distance $d$. Let $V_q(n,r) = \sum_{i \le r}\binom{n}{i}(q-1)^i$ and $t = \lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor$. Then $M \le q^{n-d+1}$ (Singleton) and $M\,V_q(n,t) \le q^n$ (Hamming). Some code has distance at least $d$ and at least $q^n/V_q(n,d-1)$ words (Gilbert-Varshamov). A [linear code](c:linear-code) of dimension $k$ has $k \le n - d + 1$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet has $q \ge 2$ symbols, and $1 \le d \le n$.
The Hamming distance of two words is the number of coordinates in which they differ.
For the linear case, $A = \mathbb{F}_q$, the code is a subspace of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$, and $M = q^k$.

conclusion: The Singleton, Hamming and Gilbert-Varshamov bounds hold, with equality in the Hamming bound if and only if the code is perfect. For linear codes, $k \le n-d+1$ and $q^kV_q(n,t) \le q^n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the triangle inequality for the Hamming distance. The proof of the Hamming bound uses it, but the three bounds are not in the declaration.

proofs.name: Projection, packing and covering
proofs.slogan: Delete coordinates for Singleton, pack disjoint balls for Hamming, and cover the space by balls around a maximal code for Gilbert-Varshamov.
proofs.scope: The four bounds. The Hamming bound has an equality clause, and the linear case follows from the first two bounds with $M = q^k$.

roles.why: The size $q$ of the alphabet gives the counts $q^n$, $q^{n-d+1}$ and $V_q(n,r)$.
The triangle inequality for the Hamming distance makes balls of radius $t$ disjoint.
A subspace of dimension $k$ has $q^k$ words, so the bounds become bounds on $k$.

steps.slogan: Count the words in a Hamming ball of radius $r$.
steps.detail: Words at distance exactly $i$ from $x$ come from choosing $i$ coordinates in $\binom{n}{i}$ ways and replacing each by one of $q-1$ other symbols. So every [ball](c:ball) of radius $r$ has $V_q(n,r)$ words.

steps.slogan: Delete the last $d-1$ coordinates and show that this map is injective on the code.
steps.detail: If two codewords agree after deleting the last $d-1$ coordinates, they differ only there, so their distance is at most $d-1 < d$. This is impossible. So the deletion map is injective, and $M \le q^{n-d+1}$.

steps.slogan: Show that balls of radius $t$ around codewords are disjoint and count them.
steps.detail: If $z$ lies in $B(x,t) \cap B(y,t)$ for codewords $x \ne y$, then $d(x,y) \le 2t \le d-1$. This is false. So the $M$ balls are disjoint subsets of $A^n$, and $M\,V_q(n,t) \le q^n$. Equality holds if and only if the balls cover $A^n$.

steps.slogan: Take a code of largest size with distance at least $d$ and show that its balls cover.
steps.detail: The codes with minimum distance at least $d$ form a finite family that contains every one-word code. Choose a code $C$ of largest size. If a word $w$ had $d(w,c) \ge d$ for all $c \in C$, then $C \cup \{w\}$ would be larger. So every word is in some ball $B(c, d-1)$.

steps.slogan: Count the cover to get $|C| \ge q^n/V_q(n,d-1)$.
steps.detail: The balls $B(c, d-1)$ with $c \in C$ cover $A^n$, so $q^n \le |C|\,V_q(n,d-1)$ by step 1.

steps.slogan: Apply the first two bounds to a subspace of dimension $k$.
steps.detail: A subspace of dimension $k$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ has $M = q^k$ words, and its minimum distance is the least weight of a nonzero word. Taking base-$q$ logarithms in $q^k \le q^{n-d+1}$ gives $k \le n - d + 1$. The Hamming bound gives $q^kV_q(n,t) \le q^n$.

steps.slogan: Collect the four bounds as the statement of the theorem.
steps.detail: Steps 2, 3, 5 and 6 give the Singleton, Hamming and Gilbert-Varshamov bounds and the linear case. All of them rest on the ball count of step 1 or on distance alone.

concepts.c:error-correcting-code: The bounds restrict the size of a code with given minimum distance.
concepts.c:linear-code: A linear code of dimension $k$ has $q^k$ words, so the bounds restrict $k$.
concepts.c:ball: Balls of radius $t$ around codewords are the objects that are packed and counted.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group with $k(G)$ [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class). The number of ordered pairs $(x,y)$ with $xy = yx$ is $k(G)\,|G|$. So two random elements commute with probability $k(G)/|G|$. If $G$ is not abelian, this probability is at most $5/8$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite.
The bound $5/8$ needs $G$ to be non abelian. For an abelian group the probability is $1$.
The bound is sharp. The dihedral group of order 8 and the quaternion group of order 8 reach it.

conclusion: The number of commuting pairs is $k(G)|G|$, and $k(G)/|G| \le 5/8$ for a non abelian group.

formal.difference: The declaration states the count $|C| = k(G)|G|$ only. This record also proves the bound $5/8$ and its sharpness.

proofs.name: Orbit-stabilizer count
proofs.slogan: Count pairs by the first entry, use orbit-stabilizer, and bound the number of classes by the size of the center.
proofs.scope: The count holds for every finite group. The bound $5/8$ holds for non abelian groups.

roles.why: Finiteness makes all sums finite and lets orbit-stabilizer count elements.
A non abelian group has a non cyclic quotient by its center, which bounds the center.
Both inequalities are equalities for the dihedral group, so the bound cannot improve.

steps.slogan: Count the commuting pairs by the first entry and apply orbit-stabilizer.
steps.detail: For each $x$, the number of $y$ with $xy = yx$ is $|C_G(x)|$, so $|C| = \sum_x |C_G(x)|$. Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation. The orbit of $x$ is its class, and the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) is $C_G(x)$. So $|\mathrm{cl}(x)|\,|C_G(x)| = |G|$.

steps.slogan: Group the sum by classes to get $|C| = k(G)|G|$.
steps.detail: A class $K$ has $|K|$ elements, and each contributes $|G|/|K|$. So $K$ contributes $|G|$. There are $k(G)$ classes, so $|C| = k(G)|G|$. Dividing by $|G|^2$ gives the probability.

steps.slogan: Bound the number of classes by the order of the center.
steps.detail: Let $z = |Z(G)|$. The classes of size 1 are the classes of central elements, so there are $z$ of them. The other $k - z$ classes have size at least 2 and hold $|G| - z$ elements. So $k \le (|G| + z)/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G/Z(G)$ is not cyclic when $G$ is non abelian.
steps.detail: Suppose $G/Z(G)$ is cyclic with generator $gZ$. Every element has the form $g^i c$ with $c$ central. Two such elements commute because $c$ and $c'$ are central. So $G$ is abelian. Thus for non abelian $G$ the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) is not cyclic.

steps.slogan: Combine the bounds to get $k/|G| \le 5/8$.
steps.detail: A group of order 1, 2 or 3 is cyclic, so $|G/Z(G)| \ge 4$ and $z \le |G|/4$. Then $k/|G| \le 1/2 + z/(2|G|) \le 1/2 + 1/8 = 5/8$.

steps.slogan: Show that the dihedral group of order 8 reaches the bound.
steps.detail: The group $D_4$ has center of order 2 and 5 classes: $\{1\}$, $\{r^2\}$, $\{r,r^3\}$, $\{s,sr^2\}$, $\{sr,sr^3\}$. So $z = |G|/4$ and $k = (8+2)/2 = 5$. Both inequalities are equalities, and $k/|G| = 5/8$.

concepts.c:conjugacy-class: The commuting pairs are counted by the conjugacy classes.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer of $x$ under conjugation is its centralizer.
concepts.c:quotient-group: The quotient by the center is the group that cannot be cyclic.

statement: Let $S$ be a set. The [free group](c:free-group) $F(S)$ is the set of words on $s^{\pm1}$ for $s \in S$, modulo cancellation of $ss^{-1}$. Every class has exactly one [reduced word](c:reduced-word). The product is the reduced concatenation. A word is the identity if and only if it reduces to the empty word. For $|S| = k$ there are $2k(2k-1)^{n-1}$ reduced words of length $n \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The set $S$ is any set, finite or infinite. Words are finite lists, and the empty word is allowed.
The count formula needs $k = |S|$ finite and $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: Each class has exactly one reduced word, the product is the reduced concatenation, and there are $2k(2k-1)^{n-1}$ reduced words of length $n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that equal reductions give equal classes. This record states the full normal form and the count.

proofs.name: Confluence of cancellation
proofs.slogan: Show that cancellation terminates and is locally confluent, so every word has a unique reduced form.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The count assumes $S$ finite.

roles.why: Words on any set can be reduced by deleting pairs, and the argument never uses the size of $S$.
The count needs $2k$ symbols to choose from.

steps.slogan: Show that every chain of cancellations ends at a reduced word.
steps.detail: Each cancellation lowers the length by 2. So every chain from a word $w$ is finite, and it ends at a reduced word.

steps.slogan: Show that two single steps from one word have a common descendant.
steps.detail: Let $w \to u$ and $w \to v$ delete pairs at positions $i$ and $j$. If $|i-j| \ge 2$, deleting both pairs gives one word $t$ with $u \to t$ and $v \to t$. If $j = i+1$, the three letters are $x x^{-1} x$, and both deletions leave $x$, so $u = v$. This is local [confluence](c:locally-confluent-relation).

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on length that all maximal chains from $w$ end at one reduced word.
steps.detail: If $w$ is reduced, the only chain is empty. Otherwise let two chains start with $w \to u$ and $w \to v$. Step 2 gives $t$ with $u \to^* t$ and $v \to^* t$. Let $r$ be a reduced word reached from $t$. By induction on the shorter words $u$ and $v$, every chain from $u$ and from $v$ ends at $r$. So every chain from $w$ ends at $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that the reduced form is constant on classes and unique in each class.
steps.detail: Call the unique word $\mathrm{red}(w)$. If $w \to w'$ then $\mathrm{red}(w) = \mathrm{red}(w')$, so $\mathrm{red}$ is constant on classes. Each class contains $\mathrm{red}(w)$. Two reduced words in one class have equal $\mathrm{red}$, and $\mathrm{red}$ of a reduced word is itself. So they are equal.

steps.slogan: Count the reduced words of length $n$.
steps.detail: A reduced word is a sequence $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of the $2k$ symbols with $x_{i+1} \ne x_i^{-1}$. There are $2k$ choices for $x_1$ and $2k-1$ for each later letter. So the count is $2k(2k-1)^{n-1}$.

steps.slogan: Read off the product and the identity test.
steps.detail: The product of classes is the class of the concatenation $uv$, whose reduced representative is $\mathrm{red}(uv)$. A word represents the identity if and only if $\mathrm{red}(w) = \mathrm{red}(\text{empty}) = \text{empty}$.

concepts.c:free-group: The group $F(S)$ is the object whose elements the theorem describes.
concepts.c:reduced-word: A reduced word has no adjacent pair $ss^{-1}$ or $s^{-1}s$.
concepts.c:locally-confluent-relation: Two single steps from one word always meet again.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $P_1,\dots,P_n$ be [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal), and let $I$ be an [ideal](c:ideal) with $I \subseteq P_1 \cup \dots \cup P_n$. Then $I \subseteq P_j$ for some $j$. Equivalently, if $I$ lies in no $P_j$, then $I$ has an element in none of the $P_j$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative with 1.
The number $n \ge 1$, and every $P_j$ is a prime ideal.
The union is finite. The result is false for infinite unions of primes in general.

conclusion: If an ideal lies in a finite union of prime ideals, then it lies in one of them.

formal.difference: The declaration is a version of the same statement for a finite set of ideals that are prime, with a small change of form.

proofs.name: Induction with a witness
proofs.slogan: Use induction on the number of primes, and build an element of $I$ outside all primes if no prime contains $I$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for finite unions.

roles.why: The sum and the product of elements of $I$ stay in the ideal $I$.
A product of elements outside a prime stays outside it.
Induction on $n$ needs a finite number of primes.

steps.slogan: Start the induction on $n$ and assume that no single $P_j$ contains $I$.
steps.detail: For $n=1$ the claim is the hypothesis. Let $n \ge 2$ and assume the claim for $n-1$ primes. Suppose $I \subseteq P_1 \cup \dots \cup P_n$ and $I$ lies in no single $P_j$. We look for a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Find $x_i \in I$ with $x_i \in P_i$ and $x_i \notin P_j$ for $j \ne i$.
steps.detail: If $I$ were in the union of the $n-1$ primes $P_j$ with $j \ne i$, the induction hypothesis would give $I \subseteq P_j$ for some $j$. This is excluded. So some $x_i \in I$ lies in no $P_j$ with $j \ne i$. Since $I$ lies in the union, $x_i \in P_i$.

steps.slogan: Case $n=2$: show that $x_1 + x_2$ lies in neither prime.
steps.detail: If $x_1 + x_2 \in P_1$, then $x_2 = (x_1 + x_2) - x_1 \in P_1$, which is false. If $x_1 + x_2 \in P_2$, then $x_1 \in P_2$, which is false. So $x_1 + x_2 \in I$ lies in neither prime.

steps.slogan: Case $n \ge 3$: put $y = x_1 + x_2 x_3 \cdots x_n$.
steps.detail: The element $y$ lies in $I$ because $I$ is an ideal. The product $x_2 \cdots x_n$ lies in every $P_j$ with $j \ge 2$, because $P_j$ contains the factor $x_j$. It lies outside $P_1$, because each $x_i$ with $i \ge 2$ is outside the prime $P_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $y$ lies outside every $P_j$.
steps.detail: If $y \in P_1$, then $x_2 \cdots x_n = y - x_1 \in P_1$, which is false. If $y \in P_j$ with $j \ge 2$, then $x_1 = y - x_2 \cdots x_n \in P_j$, which is false.

steps.slogan: Reach the contradiction and state the equivalent form.
steps.detail: So $y \in I$ lies outside all $P_j$. This contradicts $I \subseteq P_1 \cup \dots \cup P_n$. Hence $I$ lies in a single $P_j$. The contrapositive says that some element of $I$ lies outside every $P_j$ when $I \not\subseteq P_j$ for all $j$.

concepts.c:prime-ideal: Primality gives that a product of elements outside a prime is outside it.
concepts.c:ideal: The ideal $I$ is closed under sums and under multiplication by ring elements.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-[module](c:module), and $M_P$ the localization at a [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $P$. (a) An element $m$ is zero if and only if its image in every $M_P$ is zero. (b) Two elements are equal if and only if all their images are equal. (c) $M = 0$ if and only if all $M_P = 0$. (d) The same holds for $r \in R$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is commutative with 1. It may be the zero ring, which has no maximal ideals.
The image of $m$ in $M_P$ is zero if and only if $s\cdot m = 0$ for some $s \in R \setminus P$. This is the definition of the [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) of a module.

conclusion: An element, an equality, a module or a ring element is zero or equal if and only if it is so after localization at every maximal ideal.

formal.difference: The declaration states part (a) for a module. This record also states the parts (b), (c) and (d).

proofs.name: Annihilator inside a maximal ideal
proofs.slogan: Show that the annihilator of a local zero is the whole ring, because a proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal.
proofs.scope: The four parts, for any commutative ring.

roles.why: A proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal. This holds for the zero ring because its only ideal is the whole ring.
A zero image in $M_P$ gives an element $s \notin P$ with $s m = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show part (a) forward: if $m = 0$, then every image is zero.
steps.detail: The localization map is additive, so it sends $0$ to $0$ at each $P$.

steps.slogan: Show part (a) backward: suppose $\mathrm{Ann}(m) \ne R$ and reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: The [annihilator](c:annihilator) $\mathrm{Ann}(m)$ lies in a maximal ideal $P$. The image of $m$ in $M_P$ is zero, so some $s \notin P$ has $sm = 0$. Then $s \in \mathrm{Ann}(m) \subseteq P$, which contradicts $s \notin P$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $m = 0$.
steps.detail: So $\mathrm{Ann}(m) = R$. Then $1 \in \mathrm{Ann}(m)$, that is, $m = 1\cdot m = 0$. This proves part (a).

steps.slogan: Apply part (a) to $m - m'$ to get part (b).
steps.detail: The map $M \to M_P$ is additive. So $m$ and $m'$ have equal images if and only if $m - m'$ has zero image. By part (a), this holds at every $P$ if and only if $m = m'$.

steps.slogan: Get part (c) from part (a) for every element.
steps.detail: If $M_P = 0$ for all $P$, then every $m$ has zero image in each $M_P$. By part (a), every $m$ is zero. Conversely, if $M = 0$, all localizations are zero.

steps.slogan: Get part (d) by taking $M = R$.
steps.detail: The ring $R$ is a module over itself, with localization $R_P$. Part (a) with $M = R$ gives that $r = 0$ if and only if its image in every $R_P$ is zero. Parts (a), (b), (c) and (d) together give the statement.

concepts.c:module: The theorem is about elements of a module.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: Every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: The image in $M_P$ is zero when some element outside $P$ kills $m$.
concepts.c:annihilator: The annihilator of $m$ is the ideal of ring elements that send $m$ to zero.

statement: Let $w \ge 0$ be integrable on $[a,b]$ and positive on a set of positive measure. Let $\pi_n$ be the monic polynomial of degree $n$ [orthogonal](c:orthogonality) to all polynomials of lower degree. Then $\pi_n$ has $n$ simple roots $x_i$ in $(a,b)$. The rule $\sum\lambda_i f(x_i)$ with Lagrange weights is exact to degree $2n-1$, has $\lambda_i > 0$, and is never exact at degree $2n$. No other nodes do as well.

hypotheses.text: The weight $w$ is integrable on $[a,b]$, nonnegative, and positive on a set of positive measure. So every polynomial is integrable against $w$.
The nodes of a general rule in the last two claims are real. They need not lie in $[a,b]$.
The number $n \ge 1$ is an integer.

conclusion: The polynomial $\pi_n$ has $n$ simple roots in $(a,b)$, the rule with these nodes and weights $\lambda_i > 0$ is exact to degree $2n-1$, and no rule with $n$ nodes is exact to degree $2n$. Any rule exact to degree $2n-1$ uses these nodes and weights.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a polynomial of low degree equals its Lagrange interpolant. This record uses it in one step of a larger proof.

proofs.name: Orthogonality and division
proofs.slogan: Use orthogonality of $\pi_n$ to the quotient in a division by $\pi_n$ to get exactness, and a sign argument to place the roots.
proofs.scope: The five claims, for every $n \ge 1$.

roles.why: Positivity of $w$ on a set of positive measure makes the pairing an inner product on polynomials.
A general rule needs nodes with the polynomial $\prod(x-y_i)^2$ nonzero at no other points.
The degree count $2n-1$ and the division by $\pi_n$ use the same integer $n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the pairing is an inner product on polynomials.
steps.detail: Let $g \ne 0$ be a polynomial. It has finitely many roots, and $w > 0$ on a set of positive measure. So $g^2w > 0$ on a set of positive measure, and $\int g^2w > 0$. Thus $\langle f,g\rangle = \int fgw$ is an inner product, and all integrals are finite.

steps.slogan: Build $\pi_n$ by Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation and show that it is unique.
steps.detail: Apply Gram-Schmidt to $1, x, x^2, \dots$. Dividing the $n$-th output by its leading coefficient gives a monic $\pi_n$ orthogonal to all polynomials of lower degree. If $\pi$ and $\pi'$ are two such polynomials, then $\pi - \pi'$ has degree below $n$ and is orthogonal to itself, so it is zero.

steps.slogan: Show that $\pi_n$ has $n$ simple roots in $(a,b)$.
steps.detail: Let $x_1,\dots,x_m$ be the points in $(a,b)$ where $\pi_n$ changes sign, and put $q = \prod(x - x_j)$. Then $\pi_n q$ has constant sign, so $\int \pi_n q w \ne 0$ by step 1. If $m < n$, orthogonality gives $\langle\pi_n,q\rangle = 0$, a contradiction. So $m = n$, and these are all the roots, each simple.

steps.slogan: Show that the rule is exact up to degree $2n-1$.
steps.detail: Divide $f$ of degree at most $2n-1$ by $\pi_n$: $f = s\pi_n + r$ with $\deg s, \deg r \le n-1$. Then $\int fw = \langle s,\pi_n\rangle + \int rw = \int rw$. The nodes are distinct, so $r$ equals its Lagrange interpolant $\sum r(x_i)\ell_i$, and $\int rw = \sum\lambda_i r(x_i) = \sum\lambda_i f(x_i)$, because $\pi_n(x_i) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\lambda_i = \int\ell_i^2w > 0$.
steps.detail: The polynomial $\ell_i^2$ has degree $2n-2 \le 2n-1$. By step 4, $\int\ell_i^2w = \sum_j\lambda_j\ell_i(x_j)^2 = \lambda_i$, because $\ell_i(x_j) = \delta_{ij}$. The integral is positive by step 1.

steps.slogan: Show that no rule with $n$ nodes is exact to degree $2n$.
steps.detail: For any real nodes $y_i$ and weights $\mu_i$, put $f = \prod(x - y_i)^2$. Then $\sum\mu_if(y_i) = 0$, but $\int fw > 0$ by step 1. So the rule is not exact for $f$.

steps.slogan: Show that a rule exact to degree $2n-1$ has nodes $x_i$ and weights $\lambda_i$.
steps.detail: Put $\omega = \prod(x - y_i)$. For $g$ of degree at most $n-1$, the product $\omega g$ has degree at most $2n-1$. So $\langle\omega,g\rangle = \sum\mu_i\omega(y_i)g(y_i) = 0$. By uniqueness, $\omega = \pi_n$, so the $y_i$ are the $x_i$. Exactness for $\ell_i$ gives $\lambda_i = \sum_j\mu_j\ell_i(x_j) = \mu_i$.

concepts.c:orthogonality: The defining property of $\pi_n$ is orthogonality to lower degrees.

statement: Let $p(z) = z^n + a_{n-1}z^{n-1} + \dots + a_0$ with $n \ge 1$, and let $\zeta$ be a [root](c:complex-roots) of $p$. Put $a_n = 1$. (i) $|\zeta| < 1 + \max_{k<n}|a_k|$. (ii) $|\zeta| \le \max(1, \sum_{k<n}|a_k|)$. (iii) $|\zeta| \le 2\max(|a_{n-1}|, |a_{n-2}|^{1/2}, \dots, |a_1|^{1/(n-1)}, |a_0/2|^{1/n})$. (iv) If $a_0 \ne 0$, then $|\zeta| > 1/(1 + \max_{k\ge1}|a_k|/|a_0|)$.

hypotheses.text: The [polynomial](c:polynomial) $p$ is monic of degree $n \ge 1$ with complex coefficients.
In claim (iv), the constant term $a_0$ is not zero.

conclusion: Every root of a monic polynomial satisfies the Cauchy, sum and Fujiwara upper bounds, and a nonzero constant term gives the lower bound (iv).

formal.difference: The declaration states a norm inequality for products in a normed ring. The record states four root bounds and does not use that declaration directly.

proofs.name: Root inequality
proofs.slogan: Turn the root equation into one inequality for the size of the root, and derive each bound from it.
proofs.scope: The four bounds, for any complex root.

roles.why: Monic form gives $\zeta^n = -\sum a_k\zeta^k$ and so the base inequality.
A nonzero $a_0$ makes $\zeta \ne 0$ and the reciprocal polynomial well defined.

steps.slogan: Derive the base inequality $r^n \le \sum_{k<n}|a_k|r^k$ for $r = |\zeta|$.
steps.detail: From $p(\zeta) = 0$ we get $\zeta^n = -\sum_{k<n} a_k\zeta^k$. The triangle inequality gives $r^n \le \sum_{k<n}|a_k|r^k$. All bounds follow from this.

steps.slogan: Prove the Cauchy bound (i).
steps.detail: Let $\alpha = \max|a_k|$. If $\alpha = 0$, then $r = 0 < 1$. If $r \le 1$, then $r < 1 + \alpha$. Let $r > 1$. Then $r^n \le \alpha\sum_{k<n}r^k = \alpha(r^n-1)/(r-1) < \alpha r^n/(r-1)$. Dividing by $r^n$ gives $r - 1 < \alpha$.

steps.slogan: Prove the sum bound (ii).
steps.detail: Let $r > 1$. Then $r^k \le r^{n-1}$ for $k \le n-1$, so $r^n \le r^{n-1}\sum|a_k|$. Dividing by $r^{n-1}$ gives $r \le \sum|a_k|$. If $r \le 1$, then $r \le 1$. So $r \le \max(1,\sum|a_k|)$.

steps.slogan: Prove the Fujiwara bound (iii) by contradiction.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be the maximum in (iii). Then $|a_{n-k}| \le B^k$ and $|a_0| \le 2B^n$. If $B = 0$, then $p = z^n$ and $r = 0$. Let $B > 0$ and $t = B/r$. The base inequality gives $1 \le \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}t^k + 2t^n$. Suppose $t < 1/2$. The right side is $(t + t^n - 2t^{n+1})/(1-t)$, so the inequality means $(2t-1)(1-t^n) \ge 0$. But $2t - 1 < 0$ and $1 - t^n > 0$. So $t \ge 1/2$, that is, $r \le 2B$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the reciprocal polynomial when $a_0 \ne 0$.
steps.detail: Then $\zeta \ne 0$ and $w = 1/\zeta$ is a root of the monic polynomial $q(w) = w^n + (a_1/a_0)w^{n-1} + \dots + (a_{n-1}/a_0)w + 1/a_0$. Its coefficients are $a_j/a_0$ for $1 \le j \le n$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Cauchy bound to $q$ to get (iv).
steps.detail: Part (i) for $q$ gives $1/|\zeta| < 1 + \max_{1\le j\le n}|a_j|/|a_0|$. Take the inverse of both positive sides. This proves (iv). Together with steps 2, 3 and 4, this proves the statement.

concepts.c:complex-roots: The bounds are for roots of the polynomial in the complex plane.
concepts.c:polynomial: The coefficients of the monic polynomial enter every bound.
