statement:
Let $\mu,
u$ be probability vectors on a finite set $X$, and let $\kappa(\cdot|x)$, $\eta(\cdot|x)$ be probability vectors on a finite set $Y$. Put $P = \mu\kappa$ and $Q = 
u\eta$. Then $D(P\|Q) = D(\mu\|
u) + \sum_x\mu(x)D(\kappa(\cdot|x)\|\eta(\cdot|x))$ in $[0,\infty]$, where $D$ is the [relative entropy](c:relative-entropy). So $D(P\|Q) \ge D(\mu\|
u)$ and $D(P\|Q) \ge D(P_Y\|Q_Y)$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $X$ and $Y$ are finite.
The conventions are $0\log(0/q) = 0$ and $p\log(p/0) = +\infty$ for $p > 0$. Logarithms are natural. Terms with $\mu(x) = 0$ count as $0$.
The equality clause is stated only when $D(\mu\|\nu)$ is finite. Then $D(P\|Q) = D(\mu\|\nu)$ if and only if $\kappa(\cdot|x) = \eta(\cdot|x)$ whenever $\mu(x) > 0$.

conclusion: The relative entropy of joint laws is the sum of the relative entropy of the first marginals and the average conditional relative entropy. Hence it is at least that of either marginal.

formal.difference: The declaration states the chain rule for the composition-product of a measure and a kernel. This record proves the finite case with the extra marginal bound and equality clause.

proofs.name: Factor the likelihood ratio
proofs.slogan: Factor $P/Q$ into a marginal ratio and a conditional ratio, take logarithms, and sum with the weights $P$.
proofs.scope: The finite case. The same proof works for standard Borel spaces with kernels.

roles.why: Finite sums let us swap the order of summation freely.
The conventions make the infinite case and the terms with zero mass well defined.
Nonnegative terms with positive weights vanish only when each term vanishes.

steps.slogan: Show that $P \ll Q$ if and only if $\mu \ll \nu$ and $\kappa(\cdot|x) \ll \eta(\cdot|x)$ for $\mu(x) > 0$.
steps.detail: Suppose $P \ll Q$. Take $x$ with $\mu(x) > 0$ and $y$ with $\kappa(y|x) > 0$. Then $P(x,y) > 0$, so $Q(x,y) = \nu(x)\eta(y|x) > 0$. Hence $\nu(x) > 0$ and $\eta(y|x) > 0$. The converse is the same argument read backwards.

steps.slogan: Treat the case $P \not\ll Q$, where $D(P\|Q) = +\infty$.
steps.detail: By step 1, either $D(\mu\|\nu) = +\infty$ or some $x$ with $\mu(x) > 0$ has $D(\kappa(\cdot|x)\|\eta(\cdot|x)) = +\infty$. All terms on the right lie in $[0,+\infty]$, so the right side is $+\infty$ too.

steps.slogan: Assume $P \ll Q$ and factor the likelihood ratio.
steps.detail: For $P(x,y) > 0$, $P/Q = (\mu(x)/\nu(x))\cdot(\kappa(y|x)/\eta(y|x))$, and all factors are positive and finite by step 1. Taking logarithms gives the sum of two logarithms.

steps.slogan: Multiply by $P(x,y)$ and sum to prove the identity.
steps.detail: The first term gives $\sum_x\mu(x)\log(\mu(x)/\nu(x))\sum_y\kappa(y|x) = D(\mu\|\nu)$, because $\sum_y\kappa(y|x) = 1$. The second term is $\sum_x\mu(x)D(\kappa(\cdot|x)\|\eta(\cdot|x))$.

steps.slogan: Use Gibbs inequality for the bound and the equality clause.
steps.detail:
Each conditional term is at least $0$ by Gibbs inequality, so $D(P\|Q) \ge D(\mu\|
u)$. If $D(\mu\|
u)$ is finite, equality holds if and only if the weighted sum of conditional terms is $0$. This holds if and only if each term with $\mu(x) > 0$ is $0$, that is, $\kappa(\cdot|x) = \eta(\cdot|x)$. If $D(\mu\|
u) = +\infty$, both sides are $+\infty$ and the clause can fail.

steps.slogan: Swap the roles of $x$ and $y$ to bound the second marginal.
steps.detail: If some $y$ has $P_Y(y) > 0$ and $Q_Y(y) = 0$, both divergences are $+\infty$. Otherwise write $P = P_Y\pi$ and $Q = Q_Y\rho$, with any probability vector where the mass is $0$. Steps 1 to 5 give $D(P\|Q) = D(P_Y\|Q_Y) + \sum_yP_Y(y)D(\pi(\cdot|y)\|\rho(\cdot|y)) \ge D(P_Y\|Q_Y)$.

concepts.c:relative-entropy: The quantity $D$ in the identity is the relative entropy of two laws.

statement: Let $T_1,\dots,T_m$ be [independent](c:independent-random-variables) with $T_i \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_i)$, and let $\Lambda = \sum\lambda_i$. Let $T = \min T_i$. Then $P(T > t) = e^{-\Lambda t}$. The index $I$ of the minimum is almost surely unique, with $P(I = i) = \lambda_i/\Lambda$. The variables $T$ and $I$ are independent, and $E[T] = 1/\Lambda$.

hypotheses.text: The clocks are independent and have positive finite rates.
The law $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ has survival function $P(T_i > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \ge 0$.

conclusion: The minimum is exponential with rate $\Lambda$, the winner is clock $i$ with probability $\lambda_i/\Lambda$, and the minimum and the winner are independent.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the distribution function of an exponential measure. This record uses it in a larger proof about the minimum of independent clocks.

proofs.name: Minimum of exponentials
proofs.slogan: Compute the survival function of the minimum, then integrate over the winner's time to get the joint law.
proofs.scope: The four claims (a) to (d), for any finite number of clocks.

roles.why: Independence turns the survival of the minimum into a product and justifies the iterated integral.
The survival function $e^{-\lambda t}$ makes the product and the integral explicit.

steps.slogan: Compute the survival function of the minimum.
steps.detail: The event $T > t$ holds if and only if $T_i > t$ for all $i$. By independence, $P(T > t) = \prod e^{-\lambda_it} = e^{-\Lambda t}$. This proves (a).

steps.slogan: Write the joint probability of the winner and the time as an integral.
steps.detail: Fix $i$ and $t \ge 0$. The event $\{T>t, I=i\}$ is $\{T_i>t, T_j>T_i\ \forall j\ne i\}$. By independence and Tonelli's theorem, its probability is $\int_t^\infty\lambda_ie^{-\lambda_is}\prod_{j\ne i}P(T_j>s)\,ds$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the integral to get $(\lambda_i/\Lambda)e^{-\Lambda t}$.
steps.detail: Here $\prod_{j\ne i}P(T_j>s) = e^{-(\Lambda-\lambda_i)s}$. So the probability is $\int_t^\infty\lambda_ie^{-\Lambda s}ds = (\lambda_i/\Lambda)e^{-\Lambda t}$.

steps.slogan: Show that ties have probability zero.
steps.detail: For $i \ne j$, the variables $T_i$ and $T_j$ are independent with continuous laws, so $P(T_i = T_j) = 0$. A finite union of null events is null. So one index attains the minimum almost surely.

steps.slogan: Read off (b) and (c) from steps 1 and 3.
steps.detail: Put $t = 0$ in step 3 to get $P(I = i) = \lambda_i/\Lambda$. Then $P(T>t, I=i) = P(I=i)P(T>t)$ for every $t$ by step 1. The sets $\{T>t\}$ generate the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, so $T$ and $I$ are independent.

steps.slogan: Compute the mean (d) by integrating the survival function.
steps.detail: The layer cake formula writes the mean as the integral of the survival function. So $E[T] = \int_0^\infty P(T>t)\,dt = \int_0^\infty e^{-\Lambda t}dt = 1/\Lambda$.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence makes the joint probability a product of single-clock factors.

statement: Let $X$ be a normed space and $Y$ a [Banach space](c:banach-space). Let $T_n\colon X \to Y$ be [compact operators](c:compact-operator) and $T$ a bounded operator with $\|T_n - T\| \to 0$. Then $T$ is compact. So the compact operators form a closed subspace of $B(X,Y)$, and every norm limit of finite rank operators is compact. Strong convergence is not enough.

hypotheses.text: The space $Y$ is complete. This turns total boundedness into relative compactness.
The convergence is in the operator norm. Strong convergence $T_nx \to Tx$ for each $x$ does not suffice.
The domain $X$ can be any normed space.

conclusion: A norm limit of compact operators into a Banach space is compact, so the compact operators form a norm closed subspace.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the set of compact operators is closed. This record adds the epsilon-net proof and the counterexample for strong limits.

proofs.name: Epsilon over three
proofs.slogan: Approximate $T$ by a compact $T_n$, cover the image of the unit ball for $T_n$ by finitely many balls, and enlarge each ball.
proofs.scope: The statement and the example showing that strong limits fail.

roles.why: Completeness of $Y$ makes a totally bounded image relatively compact.
Operator norm convergence gives a uniform estimate on the unit ball.
Only the unit ball of $X$ enters, so any normed domain works.

steps.slogan: Reduce compactness to total boundedness of $T(B)$.
steps.detail: Let $B$ be the closed unit ball of $X$. The operator $T$ is compact if $T(B)$ is relatively compact. Since $Y$ is complete, this holds if and only if $T(B)$ is [totally bounded](c:totally-bounded-space).

steps.slogan: Choose $n$ with $\|T - T_n\| < \varepsilon/3$.
steps.detail: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Pick $n$ with $\|T - T_n\| < \varepsilon/3$. The set $T_n(B)$ is totally bounded, because $T_n$ is compact.

steps.slogan: Choose a finite net of $T_n(B)$.
steps.detail: Choose $x_1,\dots,x_N \in B$ such that the balls of radius $\varepsilon/3$ around $T_nx_1,\dots,T_nx_N$ cover $T_n(B)$.

steps.slogan: Estimate $\|Tx - Tx_i\|$ by three terms.
steps.detail: Let $x \in B$ and pick $i$ with $\|T_nx - T_nx_i\| < \varepsilon/3$. Then $\|Tx - Tx_i\| \le \|Tx - T_nx\| + \|T_nx - T_nx_i\| + \|T_nx_i - Tx_i\| < \varepsilon$. So the balls of radius $\varepsilon$ around $Tx_i$ cover $T(B)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $T$ is compact and that the compact operators form a closed subspace.
steps.detail: Every $\varepsilon$ gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $T(B)$, so $T$ is compact by step 1. Sums and scalar multiples of compact operators are compact, so they form a linear subspace, and it is closed by what we proved.

steps.slogan: Show by example that strong limits of compact operators need not be compact.
steps.detail: Let $P_N$ be the orthogonal projection of $\ell^2$ onto $\mathrm{span}(e_1,\dots,e_N)$. Each $P_N$ has finite rank, and $P_Nx \to x$ for every $x$. The limit is the identity, which is not compact on $\ell^2$, because $(e_k)$ has no convergent subsequence.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the target is used in step 1.
concepts.c:compact-operator: The operators $T_n$ and $T$ send the unit ball to relatively compact sets.
concepts.c:totally-bounded-space: A finite net for every $\varepsilon$ is total boundedness.
